lines.text: Every empire I know started with something embarrassingly small. Yours is a folding table. Good.
Tap the counter until your wrist complains. Nobody respects money they didn't sweat for at least once.
Main Street. Now people know your name, and some of them will want to borrow it.
You'll touch markets and property this chapter. Respect both; trust neither.
Raw power: fields, factories, fabric. The world runs on things before it runs on ideas.
Your first billion is near. It changes how waiters look at you. It shouldn't change how you look at them.
Old money will smile at you this chapter. Count your fingers after every handshake.
Mergers are marriages with lawyers. Choose partners whose weaknesses cover each other.
Banks, builders, broadcasters. You are no longer in business. You are the business climate.
The technologists are coming. They talk fast. Make them show you the numbers slowly.
Silicon and signal. Your empire learns to think, and then to talk back.
Two conglomerates. Remember when one kiosk felt like a lot? Keep that memory somewhere safe.
Escape velocity. Airlines lose money beautifully; cures make it quietly. Own both.
From here the numbers stop meaning anything to normal people. Make sure they still mean something to you.
The Crown. A stadium, a rocket, and then the question every founder dreads: who comes next?
Finish this, and you'll hand it all to an heir. The best thing you can leave them is a habit, not a fortune.
One chapter down. You can stop pretending the kiosk was a hobby.
Main Street is yours. The next street over is noticing.
A billionaire. Congratulations. Now act like the money is borrowed: it is, from your future self.
Old money has accepted you. That should worry you slightly.
You disrupted the disruptors. Take a day. Then don't.
You've built a group. Groups need leaders more than they need founders. Learn the difference.
Escape velocity reached. Mind the gravity on the way back down; there is always a way back down.
It's done. I've watched a lot of people build things. You built it properly.
Doors open. The first customer is the hardest. The second is just proof the first wasn't a fluke.
Sixty customers by hand. You'll never again underestimate how hard a dollar is to earn.
A real shop. Notice how the sign changed? So did your rent.
Handing over the keys is the first lesson in scale: you can't be everywhere, so hire people who don't need you to be.
A restaurant. Margins thin as a napkin. Run it well and it teaches you everything.
Weekend market. Some of my best ideas came from overhearing customers at a stall.
Momentum is the only thing in business that's free. Don't waste it.
Trucks. Unglamorous, essential. Whoever controls delivery controls the shelf.
A proper office. Resist the urge to buy an expensive chair. Buy a better spreadsheet.
Your first trade. Whatever happened, write down why you made it. Memory flatters.
A landlord now. Fix the boiler before the tenant calls. Reputation compounds like interest.
Locals love the place. That's worth more than any review.
A dispatch desk that runs without you. That's the whole trick, really. Repeat it forever.
Twenty-five million. Don't tell your old friends the number. Tell them you're doing fine.
Land. They stopped making it a while ago. Look after it and it looks after you.
A production line. Watch for the bottleneck; there is always exactly one that matters.
A balanced line hums. Learn to hear when it doesn't.
Opening night. Fashion is the only business where being late is a strategy.
Three pieces. Buy what you love; then you can never lose money, only taste.
A seat at someone else's table. Listen more than you speak. Vote less than you'd like.
Billionaire. The word sounds bigger than it feels, doesn't it?
Below the surface. Mines reward patience and punish optimism.
Power. Everyone needs it; nobody thanks the people who keep it on.
Check-in. A hotel is a promise you make every night to strangers.
Synergy. A word I hated for forty years. When it's real, it's wonderful.
Going once, going twice. Never bid with your pride. It always overpays.
Five properties. Now you're in the business of other people's homes. Be decent.
A trillionaire. There's no rulebook up here. Write a good one.
A bank. Lend to people who don't need it and you'll sleep well. Lend to people who do and you'll matter.
A treasury desk. Pick someone boring. Boring is the highest compliment in banking.
Builders. Every skyline is a list of people who were told it couldn't be done on time.
Topping out. Builders put a tree on the last beam. Find your own small ritual.
Media. You can tell stories now. Tell true ones; they age better.
Prime time has a host. Let them shine. Never let them believe they're the network.
Ten businesses. Diversified enough that a bad year in one is a footnote in all.
Shipped. The first version is always embarrassing. Ship anyway; the second is where you win.
A chief technologist. Ask them to explain it to you like you're me. If they can't, they don't understand it.
Signal. Owning the pipes is dull until everyone needs the pipes.
Full coverage. Somewhere a farmer just got a signal for the first time. Remember that one.
A group structure. Good. Now the hard part: making sure the right hand knows what the left is buying.
Wheels up. Airlines are a beautiful way to turn a fortune into a smaller fortune. Run it tight.
Flight operations in good hands. On-time departures are a moral act.
A breakthrough. Price it so the people who need it can have it. History keeps receipts.
First trials under way. Science is slow, then sudden. Fund the slow part.
Three pillars. A table needs three legs to stand. You've built a table that seats a country.
A home ground. You'll never make money on it. You'll make a city love you instead.
Season tickets sold out. Hire for character in the front office; talent is easier to find.
Liftoff. I watched the first moon landing on a borrowed television. Look at you.
A stable orbit. Steady is the hardest thing to be at speed.
Sovereign wealth. The crown is ready when you are. There's no hurry. There never really was.
A corner kiosk. Smile at every customer; half of business is remembering names.
Your first kitchen. Taste everything before it leaves the pass.
Your own trucks. Plan routes like a chess player: two deliveries ahead.
Fields of your own. Watch the weather the way traders watch the screen.
Machines don't take holidays, but the people running them should.
A label with your name on it. Brave. Make sure the seams are better than the marketing.
A mine. Safety first, second and third. Profit can wait its turn.
Power plants. Keep the lights on and nobody notices you. That's success.
A hotel. Clean sheets and a warm hello: the entire business, in one sentence.
A bank with your name over the door. Make it a name people trust with their savings.
Cranes on the skyline. Every one of them is a promise with a deadline.
A media house. Facts first. Ratings follow facts more often than people think.
A technology company. Hire people smarter than you and get out of their way.
Telecom. You're in the business of conversations now. Keep them reliable.
An airline. Every seat is a little act of trust at thirty-five thousand feet.
Pharmaceuticals. The most important business you'll ever own. Run it like it.
A sports franchise. Win with grace, lose with more of it.
A space company. The view from up there makes every border look like a pencil line.
A new tier. The sign out front gets bigger; keep the customer service the same size.
Bigger tier, bigger output. Bigger mistakes too, if you stop paying attention.
A new manager. Tell them what success looks like, then trust them to find the road.
An expansion done. Growth you planned for is the only kind that doesn't hurt.
The headquarters grows. More desks, more ideas, more meetings. Guard against the meetings.
Another conglomerate. Integration is where mergers live or die. Mind the details.
A holding company. Congratulations, you now own the thing that owns the things.
A trade done. Win or lose, ask whether you'd make it again with what you knew then.
A short covered. Betting against things is a lonely game. Don't make a habit of loneliness.
A new property. Buy the street, not just the house. Neighbourhoods move together.
Sold. The best sale is the one where the buyer also walks away happy.
Renovation done. Spend on what tenants feel: light, warmth, a door that closes properly.
Your tower is finished. Go up to the top floor once. Then go back to work.
A disaster hit one of your properties. Look after the people first; insurance will argue about the rest.
A foreclosure. It happens to the best of us. Learn the lesson; don't wear it.
A fine purchase. Things are lovely. People are lovelier. Keep that order.
You won the lot. The room will remember who outbid them. Be gracious about it.
Outbid. Good. Discipline you showed today is worth more than the painting.
The world just moved. Don't react in the first hour. Nobody knows anything in the first hour.
You sold a business. Letting go is a skill. You'll need it at the very end.
A missed payment. Call your lender before they call you. It changes the whole conversation.
Borrowed money is a tool, not a reward. Have a plan to give it back.
Loan repaid. The best feeling in finance, and the most underrated.
Taxes filed. The roads your trucks use don't pave themselves.
An audit. Clean books are boring right up until they save you.
Restructured. Pride is expensive. You just saved a fortune by setting some down.
Reborn from the ashes. I've done it twice. The second building is always better.
The crown has passed. I'll stay on for a while, if the new generation will have an old man around.
Your nemesis made a move. Rivals are useful: they show you where you're soft.
Don't hate your nemesis. Study them. Hatred is a terrible analyst.
A quarter closed. Look at what grew and what didn't, then do more of the first thing.
You've gone public. Now strangers own a piece of your dream. Treat their trust like your own money.
Collect the till before it fills; a full till is money standing still.
Managers keep the doors open while you're away. Hire one before you take a break.
Try the price levels. Too cheap and you're a charity; too dear and you're a museum.
Level ten is the first tier. Watch what happens to output when you reach it.
Frenzy is for when the counter is busiest. Save it for a rush, not a lull.
The Next Move card is your to-do list. I like to-do lists. They argue less than people do.
A second business never hurts. Restaurants pay well once their stars climb.
Expansions take time but multiply everything after them. Start them before you go to bed.
Watch income per second, not cash. Cash is a photograph; income is the film.
If you're stuck, tap. Honest work is never the wrong move in Chapter 1.
Trucks are only as good as their routes. Look at the logistics planner.
The headquarters adds slots. More slots, more businesses, more problems worth having.
Start small in the markets. Lose a little and learn a lot before you lose a lot and learn a little.
Your first property: location, location, and a tenant who pays on time.
A restaurant at level twenty-five is a neighbourhood landmark. Get there.
Dispatch managers make deliveries run while you sleep. Sleep is underrated in business.
Diversify slowly. Every new business needs attention before it pays attention back.
Keep a little cash aside. Opportunities don't send calendar invites.
The world strip shows what's moving markets. Read it like a weather report.
Decision cards are where character shows. Pick the option you'd explain to your mother.
Factories want balance. A fast line with a slow step is just an expensive queue.
Farmland rides the seasons. Plant with the cycle, not against it.
Fashion lives on launches. Time them with the trends, not your mood.
Collect a few fine things. Luxury raises your status, and status opens doors.
Board seats pay quietly. Own enough of a company and they'll ask your opinion.
Rivals are watching the Fortune list. So should you, but don't stare.
Check the tax page once a quarter. Deductions are found, not given.
Mothball a weak business if a better one needs the slot. Sentiment is not a strategy.
Credit rating matters now. Good credit is cheap money; bad credit is expensive advice.
A billion sounds like the finish line. It's barely the warm-up.
Conglomerates multiply members. Choose the merger whose parts you've already grown.
Mines and power plants reward steady investment. Don't starve them for flashier things.
Hotels fill with travellers when the world is calm. Watch the world.
Auctions run on a schedule. Know which lots you want before the gavel lifts.
Five properties is a portfolio. Spread them across cities and cycles.
Loans can accelerate a merger. Only borrow what your income can carry through a bad month.
Takeover bids come for the careless. Allies with good relationships make fine white knights.
The Desk will test your judgement. Read every option, even the ones you'll never pick.
Expansions on late businesses are expensive and worth it. Start them before long breaks.
A trillion. Somewhere, a rival is drawing up plans about you. Draw yours first.
Banks pay best with a good credit rating. Protect it like the family silver.
Construction runs on timers. Line them up so cranes never stand idle.
Media rewards consistency. A steady schedule beats a viral moment.
Ten businesses means ten managers. Upgrade the weakest one first.
Rush timers with Favor when a chapter goal is within reach, not before.
Dynasty missions refresh daily. Small wins every day add up to a big week.
Watch the weekly event. It bends the rules in your favour, if you notice it.
Sell businesses you no longer need only if the slot is worth more than the income.
The richest rivals have weaknesses. The Fortune page shows their temperament.
Technology scales fast. Feed it early and let it run.
Telecom levels add up quietly. Level twenty-five is where coverage becomes a moat.
Your second conglomerate should cover a different weakness from your first.
Market cycles turn. Rebalance when you're winning, not when you're scared.
Your tower and your best properties carry your rent. Renovate before you sell.
File taxes on time. Late filings invite the auditors, and they never leave early.
Keep a war chest for the airline. It is expensive and it will be worth it.
If a decision card feels like a trap, it probably is. Take the honest option.
Check the Store's cosmetics. Bullion earned in play buys a title worth wearing.
Airlines live on load factor. Keep the planes full and the managers sharp.
Pharma pipelines pay late and pay big. Level them before the next big push.
Three conglomerates make a holding company possible. Think about what you'll call it.
The IPO is a once-a-generation decision. Float only what you can live without.
Your heirlooms will carry into the next generation. Choose them with care.
The richest rivals are close now. They don't sleep. Neither do markets.
Space needs patience and capital. Start saving for it the day you open the airline.
Every big purchase now should have a reason you can say out loud in one sentence.
Look back at the Fortune list from Chapter 3. Then look at it now. Enjoy that for exactly a minute.
The final goal is net worth. Every business you level now pushes it a little further.
A sports franchise makes a city love you. Love is not on the balance sheet, but it matters.
The rocket will cost more than everything you built in the first three chapters. That's normal now.
Think about the heir: a trait, a Family Charter, the heirlooms. What do you want them to inherit?
Passing the crown resets the empire but not the wisdom. Legacy makes the next run faster.
A challenge run doubles the story. Try one when you're bored of winning the easy way.
Write a Family Charter you'd be proud to follow yourself.
Nothing up here is urgent. Take the decisions slowly; there's no one left to rush you.
When you're ready, the Crown screen shows what the next generation receives. Read it twice.
